clue.text: Trying situation for those who bag babies?

definitions.text: Trying situation for those who bag babies?

parts.words: Trying situation for those who bag babies
parts.note: a trial held by animals that carry their young in a pouch, read as a mock tribunal

explanation.surface: A puzzle over who has the hardest time among people who carry infants in bags.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trying' means holding a trial, not tiresome; the creatures that 'bag babies' are the marsupials that keep their young in a pouch.
explanation.definitionFit: An irregular, self-appointed tribunal that ignores due process is the idiom's meaning, with a pouched Australian animal in its name.

clue.text: Got booted to take flight, having greatness thrust upon one

definitions.meaning: literally booted so as to climb a flight of steps
promoted to a grander but less influential post, a quotation from Twelfth Night

explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means moved to a higher but powerless position, to be rid of someone; literally, booted up a staircase.

parts.note: taken as written
C and H mark the cold and hot taps on a basin

explanation.surface: Someone named Nick refuses to own a set of taps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nick' looks like a name, but it is a small cut. Taps are marked C for cold and H for hot.
explanation.definitionFit: A small V-shaped cut, nick and notch are synonyms.

clue.text: In no good shape as my turn comes to adopt the new measures

indicators.note: giving these two short words a turn rearranges their letters

parts.note: the metric system, then being introduced in place of imperial units

explanation.surface: Someone out of condition as their turn comes to take up the new units.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turn' is the anagram signal for 'as my'; 'the new measures' were the metric units Britain was adopting, and 'comes to adopt' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacking symmetry means not well-proportioned in form, an unbalanced shape.

clue.text: Who was heard rebuking his Indian nurse

indicators.note: the scolding words spoken out loud give the name

parts.note: 'O bad ayah!' is a rebuke to an ayah, an Indian nanny

explanation.surface: Someone overheard scolding a nanny in India.
explanation.walkthrough: An ayah is an Indian nursemaid, so 'O bad, ayah' is a scolding; said aloud it is the name of a minor Old Testament prophet.
explanation.definitionFit: The shortest book of the Hebrew Bible bears the name of this prophet, a 'who' in the sense of a person.

clue.text: It gives shape to what it's remarkable to take

definitions.text: It gives shape to what it's remarkable to take

parts.words: It gives shape to what it's remarkable to take
parts.note: the idiom 'that takes the biscuit' or its variant on a sponge moulds what it holds

explanation.surface: A riddle about something that moulds what is notable to receive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That takes the cake' means that is remarkable; the container that shapes the sponge as it bakes is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A baking vessel holds the batter and gives the sponge its form.

parts.note: U is upper-class, the top drawer of society, as in U and non-U
mph, miles per hour, measures speed

explanation.surface: A grunt of effort at full speed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'U' was 1950s shorthand for upper-class speech and manners, so it can stand for 'top'.
explanation.definitionFit: A short exclamation of effort or exertion is a variant of oomph.

definitions.meaning: literally head to head in French
a private conversation between two people

explanation.definitionFit: The French phrase for a private chat between two literally means head to head.

parts.note: the May Day figure dressed in a frame of foliage in English folk custom

explanation.surface: Someone called May has an Australian outback dweller.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bushman' suggests the outback, but here it is a man covered in leafy branches, paraded on May Day in English villages.
explanation.definitionFit: A traditional May Day reveller enclosed in greenery is the folk character named here.

clue.text: Mini-shirt for getting the tea (or something stronger?)

definitions.meaning: a short shirt or chemise, from Burns's Tam o' Shanter

definitions.text: for getting the tea (or something stronger?)
definitions.meaning: the famous clipper ship that raced tea home from China, and also a brand of Scotch whisky

explanation.surface: A skimpy garment worn while fetching a cup of tea, or perhaps a stiff drink.
explanation.walkthrough: Burns's witch Nannie wears a 'cutty sark', a short shift; the same name belongs to the tea clipper and to a blended whisky, the 'something stronger'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scots phrase for a short chemise names both a tea-carrying sailing ship and a whisky brand.

clue.text: Here's the rice to which Paddy has an aversion ().

parts.note: Pat is the familiar name for an Irishman, as Paddy is

indicators.note: read as a turning away, so the little word an is turned back to front

explanation.surface: An Irishman who dislikes a particular kind of rice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Paddy' looks like a rice field, but it is the familiar name for an Irishman; 'aversion', read as a turning away, sends 'an' backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Patna is a long-grain variety named after the Indian city where it was grown.

clue.text: The town is, for example, a town

parts.note: ham is an old English word for a village or homestead, seen in many place names

explanation.surface: A circular statement that a town is an instance of a town.
explanation.walkthrough: HAM is the Old English settlement word found at the end of many English place names; Egham itself is a town in Surrey, near Windsor.
explanation.definitionFit: Egham is a Surrey town on the Thames, so it is a fair example of a place of that kind.

definitions.meaning: short for preposition, a word class to which this one belongs
going inside, as in 'a move ... the house'

explanation.definitionFit: The word is a preposition of motion and also expresses entering a place.

definitions.meaning: hard ship's biscuit, the plain food issued to sailors
a sailing boat zigzags into the wind, first one way and then the other

explanation.definitionFit: Ship's biscuit is called hard tack, and a boat beating upwind changes course from side to side.

indicators.note: suggests that the two words can be made into something else by rearrangement

explanation.surface: A political doctrine that might win Simon over.
explanation.definitionFit: Support for rule by a king or queen is a principle of government.

parts.note: a painter is the rope at a small boat's bow, so freeing one means loosing it from its mooring

explanation.surface: An appeal to release an imprisoned artist.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'painter' is not an artist but the mooring line at the bow of a dinghy.
explanation.definitionFit: Loosing a rope from what it is tied to is to undo or release it.

parts.note: a skipper is one who hops, and his resting place is a cushion stuffed with hops to help sleep

explanation.surface: A ship's captain takes a nap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Skipper' looks like a captain but here is anyone who jumps; a pillow filled with dried hops was a traditional sleep aid.
explanation.definitionFit: A cushion filled with dried flowers of the beer plant was used to induce sleep.

clue.text: To peel an onion with another vegetable makes weepy

indicators.note: peeling strips the outside, so the word onion loses its first and last letters

parts.note: a bean is another vegetable

explanation.surface: Kitchen advice: peeling onions alongside other vegetables brings on tears.
explanation.walkthrough: Peeling ONION leaves NIO. Niobe of Greek myth wept endlessly for her slain children, so a Niobean person is tearful.
explanation.definitionFit: Niobe, turned to stone while weeping, gives an adjective for someone given to tears.

parts.note: a person whose arguments are clever but unsound

explanation.surface: Someone acts without proper grounds.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as 'he has no justification'; it means his reasoning itself is faulty, plausible but fallacious.
explanation.definitionFit: A specious arguer who uses clever but misleading logic is the classical word's later sense.

clue.text: Christmas fairy found here in Essex

definitions.text: Christmas fairy found here in Essex

parts.words: Christmas fairy found here in Essex
parts.note: the fairy sits at the very top of the Christmas fir; the place is a village in Essex

explanation.surface: A festive fairy figurine discovered in an Essex town.
explanation.walkthrough: The fairy perches at the tip of the tree; Tiptree is an Essex village known for its jam factory.
explanation.definitionFit: Tiptree is an Essex village, and its name describes where a Christmas fairy is placed.

parts.note: an archaic third-person form of the verb to carry or endure

explanation.surface: Ageing grizzlies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bears' looks like the animal; it is the verb, and 'Old' asks for its biblical -eth form.
explanation.definitionFit: The King James style of 'carries' adds -eth to the verb stem.

clue.text: The " loafingness of a wide boy ?

definitions.text: The " loafingness of a wide boy

parts.note: loaf gives bread and -ness gives the abstract suffix -th; a wide boy's quality is wideness

explanation.surface: The idleness of a British petty spiv.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'wide boy' is British slang for a shady dealer; here 'wide' is taken literally, and 'loaf-ness' is bread plus the noun ending -th.
explanation.definitionFit: Width or extent from side to side is the measure of how wide something is.

definitions.meaning: sandy desert ground is dry and barren

explanation.definitionFit: Dry and parched describes both a thirsty throat and desert sand.

clue.text: Asian resort's recession in the recess

indicators.note: a going back, so the word for the resort is written backwards

parts.note: a spa is a health resort
E for Eastern, standing for Asian

explanation.surface: An Asian holiday destination going downhill in an economic slump.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recession' looks economic but turns SPA into APS; 'Asian' gives E, for East.
explanation.definitionFit: The semicircular recess at the east end of a church is this architectural term.

parts.note: a bell's ringing noise, also the noise of a gaffe, since a dropped brick is a blunder called a ...

explanation.surface: Someone named Bell lets a load of bricks fall with a noise.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'drop a brick' is British slang for making a gaffe, also called 'dropping a clanger'; a bell's ring is a resonant metallic sound.
explanation.definitionFit: A loud metallic ringing noise suits both a bell and falling hard objects.

parts.note: AB, able seaman, is a naval rating
in cricket either dismissal leaves the batsman out

explanation.surface: A sailor dismissed at cricket, roughly speaking.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'rating' is a non-officer sailor; being caught or bowled are ways a cricket batsman is dismissed.
explanation.definitionFit: Roughly or around, as in 'around ten', is the sense here.

clue.text: I temporized, getting into deep water

definitions.meaning: a hesitant opening word used to stall, as in '..., I'm not sure'
a shaft sunk to reach underground water

explanation.definitionFit: The stalling interjection is also the shaft dug down to groundwater.

parts.note: the Virginia colonist who wed Pocahontas, daughter of the chief Powhatan, in 1614

explanation.surface: A bridegroom identified through his famous father-in-law.
explanation.walkthrough: Pocahontas was the daughter of Powhatan, chief of a Virginia confederacy; the English settler John Rolfe married her.
explanation.definitionFit: John Rolfe, a Jamestown tobacco planter, was the husband of Pocahontas.

clue.text: "Each lord of —-, … Shall do one crime or more. Once, every day, for ever" (Gilbert)

parts.words: Shall do one crime or more
parts.note: the curse on the baronets in a Gilbert and Sullivan operetta, whose title fills the gap after 'Each lord of'

explanation.surface: A fill-in-the-blank quotation from a Gilbert libretto about a cursed noble line.
explanation.walkthrough: The lines come from the Gilbert and Sullivan operetta of 1887, where every baronet of a Cornish house must commit a crime daily or die in agony.
explanation.definitionFit: The Cornish family seat and the operetta's title both carry the name that completes the curse.

parts.note: backing the football club known as the Wanderers, with nomads standing for wanderers

explanation.surface: A city whose people stand behind travelling peoples.
explanation.walkthrough: Wolverhampton Wanderers is an English football club; 'nomads' are wanderers, so the city is the one 'supporting' them.
explanation.definitionFit: Wolverhampton, in the English West Midlands, is home to the Wanderers football team.
